title: What you think now
hookLine: compare with what you wrote on day 759

lines: A PAGE WITH A DATE ON IT.
cards: A page with a date on it. Three or four lines, plain as a grocery list.
On day seven hundred fifty-nine, the first day of the block on death, this path asked one question before any tradition got to speak: what do you think happens when we die?
Not what you were taught, not what you ought to say. Just what came up first, even if it was a shrug, or I don't know. You dated it and put it away.
Since then came Socrates and the Gita, the Buddha and the Gospels, and others besides. Today the page comes back out.

teach.h: READ IT AS IF A FRIEND WROTE IT.
teach.b: First, read it as if a friend wrote it. Whoever wrote those lines was honest with what they had. There's no grade on that page, and none today.
Read it slowly, like a note left on the kitchen table.
Second, look for small changes, not big ones. A changed mind is rarely a conversion scene.
More often it's a word you'd now cross out, a fear that sits a little quieter, a picture you've added, a certainty gone soft at the edges, or a question you didn't have before. Those count.
Third, a teacher on changing your mind.

Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor whose notebook this path has read, wrote in his Meditations that if anyone could show him he was thinking or acting wrongly, he would gladly change, because he was after the truth, and the truth never harmed anyone.
The harm, he said, comes from staying in error and ignorance. Changing wasn't the failure; staying in error was.

teach.h: STAYING PUT IS AN ANSWER TOO.
teach.b: Fourth, staying put is an answer too. Some people reread their page and find they still think the same thing, only more clearly, or more calmly.
That isn't a failed year. A view that has met Socrates, the Upanishads, the Psalms and a year of living, and is still standing, isn't the same view it was. It's been tested.

how: Some people who keep a journal of their practice reread old entries at the end of a season or a year, and write a short note on what they think now beside what they wrote then.

o: Marcus Aurelius's private notebook of thoughts to himself
a Buddhist manual of sitting practices from India
a Roman emperor's public speeches to his army

games.q: the page and the question: tap the pairs.
p: what do you think happens when we die?
would gladly change if shown wrong
a fear that sits a little quieter

s: if your answer didn't change, the year didn't work
a view that has met many voices and still stands has been tested; staying put is an answer too.
Marcus Aurelius wrote that he would gladly change if someone showed him he was wrong
he says he seeks the truth, which never harmed anyone; the harm is in staying in error.
on day 759 this path asked for the right answer about death
it asked what you think, plainly, and said that I don't know is an answer too.

games.q: you reread your old page, and you don't agree with it anymore. what do you do with it?
o: tear it up: it was wrong.
write over it so it says what you think now.
keep it, and write the new lines beside it.
games.why: the practice keeps both: the change only shows when the two pages sit side by side.

practice: Set your page from day seven hundred fifty-nine in front of you, or remember as best you can what you thought back then. Ask the same question again, plainly: what do I think happens when we die?
Write what comes up first under the old lines, then one more line that begins, what changed is, and if nothing changed, write that, and why.

wordCard.voice: Meditations. Marcus Aurelius's notebook, where he wrote that he'd gladly change his mind if shown he was wrong, set beside your own first answer. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: what changed. Two honest pages, months apart, side by side. See you tomorrow.
